Against conventional wisdom, the Earth is NOT a perfect sphere.
The difference between the Equatorial diameter and the Polar diameter is about 23nm.
Because of this, the Earth is considered an OBLATE SPHEROID.
23 nm mile shorter round the poles
The Earth rotates around an axis called the Polar Axis.
The axis is aligned from the South Pole to the North Pole.
It rotates around this axis form West to East. (Towards the East)
The Equator
The Equator is a great circle whose plane is at right angles to the poles.
To help with navigation & positioning, charts use a grid of imaginary lines.
Including longitude (meridians) and latitude (parallels).
A Great Circle is the LARGEST circle that can be drawn on the Earth’s surface, this line will also pass through the centre of the Earth
A Small Circle is any circle on the Earth’s surface that does not pass through the centre of the Earth
Longitude is the angular distance around the world from the Prime Meridian 0°E/W (Greenwich Meridian).
This is half a great circle, the other half being 180°E/W (depending on direction from which this is reached).
All meridians of Longitude are great circles.
Your Longitude is measured up to 180° degrees EAST or WEST from the centre of the Earth with reference to the Prime Meridian which is an arbitrary datum that passes through Greenwich, in England.
The opposite meridian is called the ANTI-MERIDIAN. Together, the Prime Meridian and the Anti-meridian make a GREAT CIRCLE.
Parallels of Latitude
Your Latitude is measured in degrees NORTH or SOUTH from the centre of the Earth.
With reference to the Equator. Latitude varies from 0° to 90°.
Notes on Meridians of Longitude:
All great circles containing the Polar Axis are meridians of Longitude.
Meridians of Longitude indicate N/S direction in degrees True.
Meridians cut parallels of Latitude at 90°.
Greenwich Meridian
Is designated as Longitude 0 degrees East or West.
Is situated near London.
A Rhumb line cuts each meridian of longitude at a CONSTANT angle.
Between two points on the Earth’s surface, a Rhumb line is a constant direction, a Great Circle is not. However, the distance along the Great Circle is still the shortest.
Direction is to consider a circle laid flat and divided into 360 degrees. North is 000 degrees.
Directions are usually given as three-figure numbers, East 090 or South 180.
The exception to this is runway directions e.g.
RWY 03 or RWY 21.
True direction is measured with reference to the TRUE NORTH POLE, also referred to as the Geographic North Pole.
True direction is determined by the angle at which a track crosses the local meridian.
True tracks can be measured on a chart with the use of a protractor.
Earth’s Magnetic Field
The Earth is one huge magnet with two poles; the magnetic North Pole and the magnetic South Pole.
The Poles are where the lines of magnetic flux originate, and the flux lines create the Earth’s magnetic field.
Magnetic Pole
Magnetic direction is measured with reference to the MAGNETIC NORTH POLE, which unfortunately is not situated at the same location as the Geographic North Pole.
If a compass needle was freely suspended and not restricted by gravity, it would align itself with Earth’s magnetic flux lines. This creates challenges, one of which is MAGNETIC DIP.
Variation is the angular difference between MAGNETIC and TRUE North.
ISOGONALS are lines joining places of equal variation.
Where the East and West isogonals meet, is called the AGONIC LINE. Where variation is nil or zero.

lessons.title: Converting Between True, Magnetic And Compass Directions

content.content: True To Magnetic
Variation East – Magnetic Least
If the direction is 180°T and Variation is 25° East, then Magnetic Direction is (180-25) = 155°M.
Variation West – Magnetic Best
If the direction is 220°T and Variation is 17° West, the Magnetic Direction is (220+17) = 237°M.
Compass Deviation
Deviation is the angular difference between MAGNETIC direction and COMPASS direction.
Place a metal object too close to a compass needle and the magnetic needle will deviate towards it.
Any electrical equipment also produces a small magnetic field of their own. This can also cause the magnetic needle of the compass to deviate towards it.
In an aircraft, there is always a certain amount of deviation. The difference between the Magnetic direction and Compass direction can be found on a Deviation Card.
As with Variation:
Deviation East – Compass Least
Deviation West – Compass Best
Magnetic To Compass
Deviation West – Compass Best
If Magnetic Direction is 340°M and Deviation is 1°W the Compass Direction is (340+1) = 341°C.
Deviation East – Compass Least
If Magnetic Direction is 045°M and Deviation is 3°E the Compass Direction is (045-3) = 042°C.
True Bearing
When a straight line is drawn between two points (A-B) on a chart, the direction is expressed as a TRUE BEARING.
The direction from B to A is considered the RECIPROCAL. So True Bearings are either TO or FROM.
Magnetic Bearing
If a True Bearing is corrected for VARIATION, it is expressed as a Magnetic Bearing.
Compass Bearing
If a Magnetic Bearing is corrected for DEVIATION, it is expressed as a Compass Bearing.

If you pointed the nose of your rowboat directly towards the opposite side of a river with a strong current, it would make its way downstream before arriving at the other side (this movement is called DRIFT).
And the new direction that you are facing to account for the drift is your HEADING.
We measure drift as the angular difference between track and heading, measured PORT or STARBOARD from track.
The angular difference between Track and Heading is called the DRIFT ANGLE.
Drift is caused by wind. If we had a direct headwind or tailwind, there wouldn’t be any drift. However, this is seldom the case.
The vast majority of the time, wind approaches us from the side. If we wish to follow a track, we must place our aircraft nose into wind to allow it to compensate for the wind velocity.
This is called DRIFT CORRECTION.
If the wind is pushing the aircraft to the left of track, we must correct for it by applying LEFT DRIFT, or PORT DRIFT.
If the wind is pushing the aircraft to the right, we correct for it by applying RIGHT DRIFT, or STARBOARD DRIFT.
The easiest way, is to think which aircraft wing is further forward.
The Nautical Mile:
Defined as the length of the arc of a great circle which spans an angle of 1 minute of a degree from the centre of the Earth.
The Statute Mile:
Decreed by Law, no application in navigation.
The Kilometre:
Defined as the length of 1/10,000th of the distance between the Equator and the Poles.
Key measurements to remember:
1 Nautical Mile = 6080ft
1 Statute Mile = 5280ft
1 Kilometre = 3280ft
1 Nautical Mile = 1.85 Kilometres
1° at the Earth’s centre equates to 60nm at the Earth’s SURFACE.
Specifying Position on the Earth’s Surface:
Using Latitude (N & S) and Longitude (E & W)
° for degrees 1° = 60 mins of arc

Airspeed – speed of the aircraft relative to the air.
Groundspeed – speed of the aircraft relative to the ground.
Airspeed is further split up into several types.

NOTE: Speed and Velocity are different, Speed is a scalar quantity meaning it only has a magnitude (100kts), Whereas Velocity is a vector quantity meaning it has magnitude and direction. (100kts North)
[NO CONTENT IN SOURCE]
The key difference between IAS and TAS is Density.
If an aircraft was flying sea level on a standard day, its IAS and TAS would be the same.
However, as the aircraft climbs, it enters an atmosphere which is decreasing in air density the higher it climbs.
Indicated/True Airspeed Relationship:
Remember that IAS is a measurement of DYNAMIC PRESSURE.
As the aircraft climbs into less dense air, there is less air to produce this dynamic pressure, which means this pressure will want to decrease.
In order to produce the same amount of dynamic pressure (IAS) as at sea level, the aircraft must fly faster through the air (↑TAS).
Hence, TAS will increase for a given IAS if density becomes less.
True Airspeed Variations:
True airspeed is affected by the density of the air. Density will change with temperature, pressure and altitude.
Temperature – Cold air is more dense than warm air.
When it’s warm, an aircraft must travel faster for the same number of molecules per second to impact it, to maintain the same IAS.
Pressure – As the aircraft climbs, the pressure and density of the air reduces.
If you maintain the same indicated airspeed with an increase in altitude you will have increased your true airspeed.
Vectors are a line which can be used to represent a speed and direction.
The three we use which become the Triangle of Velocities are:
Heading/TAS
Track/Groundspeed
Wind speed/Direction
By adding vectors quantities, we can arrive at a resulting vector.
For example, if we add our Wind vector to our Track/Groundspeed vector, our resultant will be Heading/TAS.
Care must be taken when interpreting the wind velocity during the planning stages of a flight.
Some velocities can be given to the pilot in °T whilst others in °M.
Wind Components:
Can be given as either a + for tailwind, or - for headwind.
In aviation, speed is measured in Nautical Miles per hour, or Knots.
An aircraft travelling 60kts will cover 60nm in one hour.
If one hour is 60 minutes, then at 60kts, we will travel 1nm per minute.
This means at 120kts we will travel 2nm per minute.
Remember this for future calculations!
Other Terminology which must be remembered:
Flight-planned Track – planned path of the aircraft over the Earth’s surface.
Required Track – the intended track required to be flown to reach a certain point once off track.
Track-Made-Good – the actual path the aircraft has taken over the surface of the Earth.
Wind Angle - the angle between the wind direction and track.
Wind Correction Angle - the correction angle to allow for drift to fly a flight-planned track.
Height – The vertical distance of a level, a point or an object, measured from a specified datum.
Altitude – The vertical distance of a level, a point or an object, measured from mean sea level (MSL).
Mean Sea Level – The average level of the sea. Where altitude is measured form.
Ground Level – The level of the Earth’s surface. (This is a datum)
Elevation – The height of the ground above mean sea level.
Indicated Altitude – Is the altitude of the aircraft shown on the altimeter if correct QNH has been set.
Calibrated Altitude – Is indicated altitude corrected for instrument and position error.
Pressure Altitude(PA) – Means an atmospheric pressure, expressed in terms of altitude, which corresponds to that pressure in the standard atmosphere.
Density Altitude(DA) – Is the altitude in the ISA which has the same air density as the actual altitude.

lessons.title:
The Effect of Change in Air Temperature to Altimeter Readings
True Altitude

content.content: Temperature also has an effect on altitude.
The altimeter is built to work on ISA, which assumes a standard pressure lapse rating of 1 hPa for every 30ft you climb/descend.
Temperature will vary this lapse rate. If the air is warmer the altimeter will underreads. Showing that you are lower than the actual altitude.
If the air is colder it overreads. Showing that you are higher than the actual altitude.
The Effect of Change in Air Pressure to Altimeter Readings
As MSL pressure can vary from area to area we need to look at what happens when we fly to areas with different QNH values.

If we were to fly from Auckland(AA) at 6,500' with AA QNH set at 995hPa to Gisborne(GS) which has a QNH value of 1020hPa, and maintain 6,500' for the flight, we will have actually been in a steady climb with respect to sea level.
The reason for the steady climb is that the altimeter is set to 995hPa, but it will now be reading GS QNH values.
If we were to fly the reverse route, the opposite will occur, and we will have maintained a steady decrease in height.
This can cause problems with terrain clearance if you are tracking over areas of high terrain and flying at low cruising levels.
The Effect of Pressure on Altimeter Readings
If MSL pressure was the same everywhere, then no matter where we were, we would always be reading true height AMSL.
However, MSL pressure varies from area to area, and if the pressure datum we have our altimeter set to is no longer co-located with the MSL, then our true height above MSL will be wrong.
If the QNH is not corrected:
When flying from high pressure to low pressure, the altimeter will over-read
HI – LO - HI
When flying from low pressure to high pressure, the altimeter will under-read
LO – HI - LO
High to Low, Lookout Below
QNH – Setting QNH will set the sea level pressure in the subscale window, which will allow the altimeter to read height AMSL - Altitude.
QFE – Height above a datum. If you set your altimeter to zero on the ground, the subscale window will now read the aerodrome pressure, and your height will now read above this pressure level.
QNE – Setting 1013 in the subscale window will allow the aircraft to read pressure altitude. These are commonly referred to as Flight Levels.
QFF – Not used in New Zealand
Cruising Levels
VFR flights operating at more than 3000FT above the surface must be flown at an appropriate altitude as per the Table Of Cruising Levels.
When your MAGNETIC TRACK is between 270°M and 089°M you should cruise at Odd thousands of feet plus 500.
When your magnetic track is between 090°M and 269°M you should cruise at Even thousands of feet plus 500.
Transition Layer
The layer between transition altitude and transition level.
Within the New Zealand domestic Flight Information Region (FIR), there is an airspace which cannot be used for level cruise flight unless instructed otherwise.
This layer sits between the Transition Altitude and the Transition Level.
For large aircraft flying long distances in short periods of time well above the height of any terrain, having to continuously change the QNH would be tedious and unnecessary.
For this reason, once aircraft climb above 13,000ft (Transition Altitude) they simply set 1013 and read Flight Levels.
On descent through FL150 (Transition Level) they must set the local QNH.
In between the two is called the Transition Layer.
Aircraft flying between 13000ft and the transition level of FL150 to maintain vertical position by reference to the altimeter setting as advised by ATC.
Altimeter Setting Rules
Flight Level (FL) – When flying above 15,000’, to maintain vertical position, aircraft fly at Flight Levels with reference to standard pressure value of 1013.2hPa.
Transition Altitude – Is the altitude (13,000') at which you set 1013.2hPa when you going to be flying at Flight Levels.
Transition Level – Is the altitude at which you set the aerodrome QNH when descending from a Flight Level to operate at or below 15,000’.
Altimeter Setting Rules
Within the New Zealand FIR, Civil Aviation Rule Part 91.239, requires:-
Aircraft flying at or above the transition level of FL150 to maintain vertical position by reference to 1013.2 HPa.
Aircraft flying at or below 13000ft to maintain vertical position by reference to the QNH altimeter setting.
These altitudes were changed from the older altitudes of 11000ft/FL130 on 25 November 2004 by CAANZ.

The Sensible Horizon is the horizon tangential to a person standing on the surface of the Earth.
The Visible Horizon is slightly curved due to the curvature of the Earth. The visible horizon will also increase the higher above the sea level you are.
Be mindful of this if you are flying at altitude, it may still appear there is plenty of daylight remaining but the ground may very well already be in darkness!
Sunrise – when the upper limb of the sun is on the visible horizon.
Sunset – when the upper limb of the sun disappears below the visible horizon.
Sunlight – the period in between.
Not to be confused with Daylight.
Morning Civil Twilight – when the centre of the rising sun is 6° below the sensible horizon.
Evening Civil Twilight – when the centre of the setting sun is 6° below the sensible horizon.
Daylight – period in between. Note that daylight is always longer than sunlight.
The world is divided into time zones annotated from A to Z.
New Zealand is in the M (Mike) zone, which means we are +12 ahead of Z (Zulu) time.
Zulu time is taken from the Prime Meridian in Greenwich. It is otherwise known as Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) or Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

As mentioned, New Zealand is +12 hours ahead of UTC. However, we also must take into account the period of Summer where we place our clocks one hour forward. This gives us two different standards of time.
New Zealand Standard Time (NZST) = +12 hours
New Zealand Daylight Time (NZDT) = +13 hours
Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)
Is a coordinated system of time, used worldwide. The datum which UTC is based off is the Prime Meridian or zero degrees Longitude.
Global positioning systems are totally dependent on UTC.
Standard Time (NZST)
To avoid minor time differences due to small differences in longitude in New Zealand, the 180° meridian is our reference.
This time is referred to as New Zealand Standard Time.
NZST is precisely 12 hours ahead of UTC, making conversions between the two times somewhat easy.
Daylight Time (NZDT)
Due to Daylight Saving, our clocks are advanced 1 hour which means that we then become 13 hours ahead of UTC.
During this period time is referred to as New Zealand Daylight Time, which runs from 2am on the last Sunday in September to 3am on the first Sunday in April.
NZ first introduced Daylight Saving time in 1927. The current times were introduced and fixed by Governing Legislation in 2007.
Time is represented in 24 hour format. Combined with the date we have six, eight, ten and twelve figure date/time groups.
Six-figure – 24th at 1pm becomes 241300
Eight-figure – 16th March at 8am becomes 03160800
Ten-figure – 15th June 2021 at 2pm becomes 2106151400
Twelve-figure – 8th July 2016 8pm becomes 201607082000
Factors Affecting Sunrise And Sunset
As we know, the sun rises and sets at different times of the year.
This is due to the effect of date and latitude.
Seasons – In Summer, Morning Civil Twilight (MCT) begins EARLIER when compared to Winter, meaning the sun will rise earlier.
And in Summer, Evening Civil Twilight (ECT) starts LATER when compared to Winter, meaning the sun will set later.
Latitude – On the diagram below, you can see that points A, B and C are all on the same meridian of Longitude but are on different Latitudes.
This causes them to have different times of sunrise and sunset.
Factors Affecting The Duration Of Twilight
In the Tropics, the sun rises and sets at almost 90° to the horizon making the period of Twilight quite short.
At higher Latitudes towards the Poles, the sun rises and sets at more oblique angles, causing the period of Twilight to be longer.
Twilight is always longer in the South of the country and shorter in the North
Equatorial regions experience a very short Twilight. Poles experience a much longer Twilight.
As mentioned before, be mindful if you are flying at altitude late in the day, as you may easily be able to see the Sun well above the visible horizon, but on the ground it may have already set.
Also be mindful of any obstructing terrain. Flying on the eastern side of the Southern Alps in the late afternoon for example will slip into darkness much sooner than the West Coast.
Relationship Between Time and Longitude
In one day, the Earth rotates through 360° with reference to the Sun.
Time is a measure of the rotation of the Earth. For every hour, the Earth rotates through 15°.
Suppose the sun is directly overhead, for every point along the same meridian of longitude the Sun will be at its highest point in the sky for that day.
Looking at the North Pole at Noon, you can see the Sun is directly on the horizon.
One hour later the Earth has turned through 15° and the Sun is now overhead a meridian of longitude 15° further West.

Difficulties Of Representing A Spherical Shape On A Flat Surface
Shapes, distances, angles, and areas of the original spherical surface will always be distorted on the flat surface of a chart.
Charts are scaled down versions of the Earth’s surface, initially reducing the size of the globe to a fraction of its size then using a PROJECTION to lay it flat.
Scale
Chart scale is defined as the ratio of a given chart length to the actual distance on the Earth that it represents.
Scale = Chart length
Earth distance
The greater the CHART length for a given Earth distance, the larger the scale and therefore the more detail the Chart can provide.
A Visual Planning Chart
A VPC Chart is used for your pre-flight planning. Is a chart of the whole country on a scale of 1:1,000,000 (Small scale)
A Visual Navigation Chart
Is used for your in-flight navigation. The whole country is broken down into 16 different areas and these charts have a scale of 1:500,000 and 1:250,000.(Large scale)
An Aerodrome Chart
The Aerodrome Chart comes from the AIP. Shows the layout and facilities of the aerodrome.

Method of Indicating Relief
To distinguish between different types of terrain and ELEVATION, relief shading is used on the charts.
Lakes and rivers are in blues.
Shades of green to show low elevation.
Forested areas are shown in dark green.
Mountainous areas are represented by darker shade of brown, and also by silver to show areas of permanent snow and PEAKS.

Calculating Wind in Flight
Just work backwards from before.

The overall lesson to be learnt is ultimately AIRMANSHIP.

A position line is a line of which an aircraft is known to be on at a particular time, like a road or power line. Not as accurate as a fix because you can’t pinpoint your position, but useful for groundspeed checks.
A position fix, is when you have more than one feature or ‘check point’ to determine your location accurately.
A checkpoint is a planned feature along your route that you are expecting to see at a given time.
A waypoint is simply a name for a place in the world, that you pass along your route. Whether it be a destination, turning point, or even just a check point along your track.
e.g., “We will be flying via this waypoint”
Proper Flight Planning requires that you check:
Weather
NOTAMs
Tracks/Altitudes/Checkpoints/Turning Points
Alternates
AIPs
Aircraft pre-flight
Charts
ECT
Fuel Requirements
Airspace
Navigation Log
Equipment
One situation that could occur in the air is becoming unsure of your POSITION.
When lost, read Ground to Chart.
Climb as high as the cloud base or known airspace will let you.
Only if you were sure of your position within the last few minutes.
Reverse your track and retrace your steps to your last known. position (But don’t forget to write down your original heading).
Use local knowledge, find yourself over easier to navigate terrain.
In New Zealand, much of the land mass runs NORTH to SOUTH which leaves the EAST to WEST dimension relatively narrow.
So, if you find yourself lost in the middle of the island, try flying out to one side and using a coast to find the nearest airport.
4. Adopt the Lost Procedure.
Work out a ‘dead reckoning position’ (DR Position).
Draw lines 30° either side of your track, originating from your last fix.
Mark where you think you should be given how fast you have been flying for as long as you have been lost. This point is your Most Probable Position (MMP).
If you then mark points 10% of the distance, either side of your MMP, the space between these two points is your Most Probable Area (MPA).
Or draw a circle around your MPP, 10% of the distance. To find your MPA
Consider the following;
How much fuel do you have left?
How long until ECT?
What is the weather forecast to become?
How long has it been since you were sure of your position?
What is the condition of yourself and the aircraft (How long have you been flying for?
Have you got any food or survival equipment?
Is the aircraft operating normally?
If all else fails…
If you are 100% lost.
The last step in the recommended lost procedure is to contact some form of ATC.
Provided that you are high enough, you have a good chance of being picked up by radar.
If you believe your situation is serious enough, squawk 7700 and call for Radar Vectoring/Assistance back to Whanganui.
Aircraft Management
Balanced Flight.
Flying at Planned Airspeed/Altitude.
Altitude selection factors.
Trimming.
Lookout.
Assessing weather conditions.
Aircraft Management
SAFDIE Checks
S-Suction
A-Alternator/Altitude
F- Fuel
D-DI/Compass
I-Icing/Carb heat and check Outside Air Temp
E-Engine Ts And Ps
Maintaining A Flight Log
To keep an up-to-date flight log is easy if the necessary planning has been carried out.
Remember to record the following items:
Actual time of departure.
Position fixes- the position and time at that point.
Actual times of arrival.
ETAs and revised estimates at all checkpoints recorded in the appropriate places on the flight log.
Turning (Enroute) Points
A turning point is a place where a change of heading is required.
Make sure these are clearly marked on the charts and are recorded on the flight log with the new heading required.
Also, it is important to note the time you reach each point so you can work out the ETA for your next point.
Approaching/Rejoining Destination Aerodrome
When approaching your destination aerodrome, it is important you are prepared.
You should have an up-to-date flight log with an ETA for that aerodrome.
The AIP should be open at the correct chart and you should be familiar with the arrival procedures and layout of the aerodrome.
The correct QNH needs to be set and appropriate radio calls made.
Chart Reading Techniques
Successful chart reading depends on four things.
A knowledge of direction.
A knowledge of distance.
A knowledge of groundspeed.
The selection and identification of landmarks and checkpoints.
To make chart reading easier for yourself, pick landmarks and checkpoints that will stand out and can be easily identified while flying.
To do this, take the following factors into account when picking checkpoints.
In flight visibility.
Dimensions of the feature.
Relationship to other features.
Angle at which being observed.
Plan view of the feature if flying high.
Elevation and side view if flying low.
Pinpointing Your Position
To be able to pinpoint your position requires well selected landmarks, the chart orientated for the direction of travel.
This means that features shown on the right of track drawn on your chart will appear on the right of the aircraft’s track.
And constantly referring from the chart to what is happening outside the cockpit.
Amending ETA
During each leg of a cross country trip, you will have picked certain points where you will carry out GS checks.
From this information you can work out a new ETA by using the new GS and working the distance to go to the next point get yourself a current ETA.
Remember to record this in your flight log and pass it onto an ATS unit if needed.
Checkpoints Over or Near Mountainous Terrain.
Intervals between checkpoints.
Checkpoints and Dead Reckoning.
Chart Orientation in the cockpit.
9 mile out points
Cruise Procedures
TOC Checks. Mental calculations for Time, Dist., G/S, ETA
Cruise Routine
Once established in the cruise there are a number of things to be done.
Check that area QNH is set.
Set cruise power and correct mixture setting and trim the aircraft.
Carry out SAFDIE checks.
Obtain a position fix to confirm whether the planned track has been achieved and check the estimate for the first planned checkpoint.
Track/Heading Corrections
Track Error.
Closing Angle.
Total Correction.
Drift Lines.
1 in 60 Rule
The 1 In 60 Rule is navigation method used to determine TR and HDG changes.
The 1 in 60 Rule is based on the assumption that;
1 NM subtends an angle of 1° at a distance of 60 NM.
Therefore:-
-5nm subtends an angle of 5° at 60nm.
-10nm subtends an angle of 10° at 60nm.
-15nm subtends an angle of 15° at 60nm.
To use the 1 in 60 rule its not necessary to cover 60nm.
For example:-
4nm off track in 30nm along track is the same as
8nm off track in 60nm along track, i.e., track error = 8°
Distance Off: 10 nm
Track Error = 12°
To work out Track Error, there is a simple formula:
TE = Distance off x 60
Distance gone
Example:-
You have travelled 50nm and find out you are 10nm off track.
TE = 10/50 x 60 = 12° track error.
This can be shown on the Flight Computer:
60 nm
Distance Gone: 50 nm
Closing Angle
So far, we have used the 1 in 60 rule to work out our Track Error, but it can also be used to find the closing angle, once the point to rejoin the planned track has been selected.
To work out CA, we can use the same formula as we did for TE.
CA = Distance off x 60
Distance to go
Once TE and CA are known, the Total Correction (track change) required (TE + CA) can be determined.
This Total Correction should return the aircraft to the flight planned track at the chosen point.
This will only work if TE and CA are each no greater than 15°.
Example
An aircraft planned track A-B is 100nm long.
After 30nm on a constant heading, the aircraft is 4nm to the right of track. What is the alteration of heading to regain track:
In another 30nm?
At point B?
Total correction is TE + CA, 8° + 8° = 16° Track Correction to the left.
B) TE is still 8°
Total correction is TE + CA, 8° + 3.4° = 11.4° Track Correction to the left.
CA 8°
TE 8°
100 nm
B
A
4 nm
70 nm
30 nm
30 nm
Estimation of Heading to Make Good a Reciprocal Track
There will be occasions in your flying when you have to do a 180° turn and go back the way you came due to weather or many other reasons.
Here is a simple method to ascertain your required heading.
If you have applied left drift before turning around, fly the reciprocal HDG and deduct twice the drift.
If you have applied right drift before turning around, fly the reciprocal HDG and add twice the drift.
See diagram next page
Diverting from the Pre-planned Route
On occasions you will be required to divert to an alternate aerodrome or divert from flight plan route due to weather or passenger illness, or any number of reasons.
If the diversion requires a small heading change you can use the one in sixty method.
Example – You are tracking 320° M towards your destination, which is 135nm further on, at 133 kts GS, when you decide to divert due to bad weather.
You decide to divert and land at a small aerodrome located 10nm abeam and to the right of the planned track, 42nm ahead of your current position.
Calculate the approximate HDG and EET to arrive overhead the alternate aerodrome.
HDG required = 320°M + 14° = 334°M
ETI = 42nm at GS 133kt = 19min
If you are diverting around thunderstorms or other en-route obstacles you can use the 60° diversion method.
Divert off track by 60°, note the new heading on the flight log. Maintain this HDG for a suitable time.
If needed, parallel the original track by altering HDG by 60°, once again maintain HDG for a suitable time.
3. After the obstacle has been cleared by a suitable margin, alter HDG by a further 60° or by 120° if no parallel leg was flown.
4. When track has been rejoined, alter HDG by 60° to maintain it.
Navigation at Low Level
Navigation usually carried out at 500ft AGL, Basically the same as procedures used at higher altitudes but with some special considerations.
When flying at low levels, you must be especially careful to maintain a constant lookout due to proximity of terrain and obstacles.
A thorough study of the appropriate charts before departure is important and selection of suitable ground features made, remember you will see things in elevation rather in plan view.
Height of check features, compared to the general level of the surrounding terrain is a significant consideration for low level flight.
The use of radio masts, factory chimneys and church steeples can be used at low level.
During low level flight it is not possible to keep an as up-to-date flight log as you usually would, because of the need to give greater attention to aircraft handling.
This means your preparation will have to be thorough.
Navigation in Reduced Vis
Avoid the situation.
Resist the temptation to climb up through gaps in cloud.
Checkpoints harder to see until overhead.
Entering poor visibility configuration, account for this in your EET. Round off speed values for quick mental calculations; 1.5NM – 2NM per minute.
Frequently check your HDG, DI, Compass checks.
Chart use: Pinpoints – be accurate, make sure you know exactly where you are before pinpointing it down.
Diverting in poor visibility:
Practical diversion calculations.
If inland, draw a track to the coast.
Talk to ATS.
Use of GPS, don’t rush. (use in addition to visual navigation).
Maintain airmanship.
Uncertain of Position
Check DI and Compass.
Estimate track correction to make good TR.
If you have maintained the wrong HDG due incorrect visual reference, then recalculate.
Lost Procedure
If you become uncertain of your position, providing you have an up-to-date flight log you will be able to calculate a DR position.
If this does not help and you become totally lost the most important thing is to not panic and formulate a definite plan of action.
Causes.
Altitude.
Reverse Track.
Geography.
Air Traffic Services.
Maintain present HDG if possible.
If the next checkpoint is not in view at ETA, continue to maintain HDG for a further 10% of the total elapsed time flown since last positive fix.
Check HDGs flown since last positive fix ensuring that:
- the DI (DGI) is aligned.
- variation and drift have been applied correctly.
- a comparison of the track on the chart and that on the flight plan don’t reveal any errors.
4. Determine DR position using latest TR and GS information to establish distance flown since last fix.
Once the most probable area has been worked out, determine the minimum safe altitude and look out around the aircraft for significant features.
When a fix is obtained re-check DI and then continue with normal navigation procedures.
DR Position
To establish your DR position, you use the latest TR and GS information to work out the distance flown from your last position fix.
This new position becomes your Most Probable Position.
To get your DR position you can use two different methods.
Method 1 – Use the MPP and apply + and – 10% of the estimated distance flown since the last fix to an arc 30° either side of the probable TMG.
Method 2 – Using the most MPP draw a circle with radius equal to 10% of the estimated distance flown since the last positive fix.
Navigation in Mountainous Terrain
Mountain flying involves crossing hills, dealing with challenging weather and terrain.

Common causes of accidents include inadequate flight preparation, poor navigational techniques, misunderstanding of the weather and insufficient fuel to allow for a change of track around the high terrain.
Experience is crucial for safe mountain flying. Skills must be developed gradually, as effective navigation in mountains require practice and knowledge of techniques.
Pinpointing difficulties – harder in the mountains especially in snow covered mountains covering unique shapes and features.
Use of peaks – Tempting to point at a Mt peak, but could be the wrong peak, check your DI and compass to confirm.
Wind, drift, leeward and windward – stay windward as much as possible.
Cloud – Common in mountains, can be disorientating, minimized by coordination of visual orientation and DI/Compass readings.
Temptation to follow wider valley – Often diverge from common junction, check orientation of valleys with DI and compass.
False horizon – easy to mistake top of ridge as horizon, monitor instruments to confirm
Power limited – Power is limited at altitude, affecting your ability to climb out of high terrain
Unable to judge weather in the distance.
Therefore:
Preflight preparation.
Obtain through Met Briefing.
Operational Briefing.
Prepare flight plan.
Allow plenty of daylight.
Flight Planning/SARTIME
Lodged by telephone, internet or fax.
SARTIME vs ETA.
Updating/Terminating SARTIME.
Estimate an Aircraft Position given Bearing and Distance from a Ground Position
To work out an aircraft’s position given a bearing and a distance is quite simple.
You will be told the bearing from a ground position and the distance away from that position.
Then you transfer that information onto the chart.
You have a bearing of 360°T from NZFL at 10nm.
You plot this information on your chart to get your position.
Instructor to demonstrate.
Calculate Maximum Holding Time
When working through fuel requirements in the flight plan you will be given the holding consumption rate.
Once you have calculated the fuel required for the entire flight you can then plan your holding fuel requirements.
Remember you legally need ½ hour reserve, you also need to take into account the amount of fuel it will take to reach your alternate aerodrome.
Any more fuel added over this amount will become the fuel available for holding.
To work out how much time you have to hold will require a simple calculation on the navigation computer.
Estimated Time Of Departure (ETD)
Used for flight planning purposes. Is the estimated time you think you will get airborne.
Actual Time Of Departure (ATD)
Is the actual time you get airborne.
Estimated Elapsed Time (EET)
Is the time it takes to fly from point A to point B.
Estimated Time Interval (ETI)
Is the time from when you make one reporting call to the next call.
For example, you make a radio call to DUD Tower saying FGC is Middlemarch 5000` time 00 will call again at 30.
The ETI is the time between the two calls.
Estimated Time Of Arrival (ETA)
The time at which you think you will arrive at your destination.
Actual Time Of Arrival(ATA)
The actual time you arrive at your destination.
Position Reference Methods
There are several methods used.
Place Name – FGC is overhead Dunedin airport.
Bearing and Distance – FGC is 5 miles to the west of Dunedin airport.
Latitude and Longitude – FGC is Latitude S 45°56` and Longitude E 170°12`.
The Grid System – A chart can be broken up into several grids, position is given by stating what grid you are in.

Globe
Handout
Route Selection
When selecting a route there are several things to consider. Firstly weather, you want to fly a route that has relatively settled weather.
The ground elevation needs to be looked at, to see if the aircraft has the performance to climb over high terrain.
Choose a route that you feel comfortable flying.
If you have no mountain flying experience for example you don’t want to pick a route that involves flying in mountainous terrain.
With everything you do in aviation it’s a commonsense approach and that’s what is needed when selecting a route.
South Island Trip, route selection esp in NFO
Selecting Altitude
When selecting an altitude to fly at you should always cruise at altitudes consistent with the VFR magnetic track-altitude requirements.
NOSE
Selecting Alternate Routes And Aerodromes
If you must select an alternate route, considerations are the same as for selecting your original route.
When choosing alternate aerodromes, you need to consider, the fuel facilities they have, is it suitable for the aircraft you're flying and do you need permission to land there.
Chart Preparation
Once you have you have completed your pre-flight planning it is a good idea to transfer some of the details onto the chart.
Let's say you were planning a flight from Dunedin to Wanaka, Queenstown and back to Dunedin.
Mark down on the chart your departure aerodrome Dunedin, your turning points of Wanaka and Queenstown and the destination aerodrome Dunedin.
Draw your track lines in pencil making them nice and thick so they stand out.
Where you plan to update your ETAs, put a mark on the chart to remind yourself.
Instructor will demonstrate how to fully prepare a chart.

Globe
Handout
Flight Plan for a VFR Cross-country
The easiest way to show how to complete a flight plan is to go step by step through a real-life example.
Plan a daytime VFR flight from Hokitika airfield (NZHK) to Omaka airfield (NZOM). The flight is to be via Reefton (42°07’S 171°52’E). The ETD is 2215 UTC.
Flight Plan Details
Climb
Set HDG overhead HK at 1500’ AMSL and climb on track to an altitude of 7500’.
Mean Rate of Climb 700 fpm.
CAS 75kts
Cruise
CAS 90kts
Descent
Descend on track to arrive overhead OM at 1500’ AMSL
Mean Rate of Descent 600 fpm
CAS 75kts
GA Forecast Wind Velocities And Temperatures
Hokitika-Reefton Reefton-Omaka
With that information we can now complete part of the flight plan.
From/To
In this column enter the different legs for the flight e.g., HK/TOC, TOC/RTN, RTN/TOD, and TOD/OM.
CAS kt
For each leg we have been given the CAS value so you can put this into the flight plan.
Temperature And Altitude
Climb
The climb is from 1500 to 7500 ft = 6000 ÷ 3 = 2000 ft.
Deduct 2000 from 7500 = 5500 ft = mean (2/3rd up) climb altitude.
The temperature at 5500 ft is +8°, this is now placed in the temperature column.
Cruise
The level cruise from TOC to RTN at 7500 ft has a temperature of 3.5° and from RTN to TOD at 7500 ft has a temperature of 4°.
Descent
During the descent from 7500 ft to 1500 ft AMSL, We descend through 6000 ft so the descent altitude will be, 6000 ÷ 2 = 3,000.
Add 3000 to 1500 = 4500 ft which is our descent altitude.
The temperature at 4500 ft is 11°.
This information is added to the flight plan form.
Climb/Descent Altitudes And Time
Climb
For the climb we start at 1500 ft and climb to 7500 ft = 6000 ft at 700 fpm = 8.6 minutes = 9 minutes rounded off to the nearest minute. Enter this into the time column.
Descent
The descent is from 7500 ft to 1500 ft = 6000 ft at 600 fpm = 10 minutes. Enter this into the time column.
TAS
Using CAS, Temp and Altitude information you can work out your TAS for each leg.
Instructor to demonstrate.
Once this has been found out, enter this into the TAS column.
Tracks And Distances
To measure the track, use a protractor, instructor to demonstrate. At the same time, you can measure the distances using a navigation ruler.
Two total distances are ‘hooked’ as shown on the flight plan.
Once the GS is known it is a simple matter to calculate climb and descent distances which allows us to determine the level cruise sectors of each track.
Wind Velocities
The wind velocities are taken from the GA weather.
Climb Wind
The wind at 5500 ft is determined by interpolation between
The difference between 210 and 200 = 10° in 2000 ft
Thus, the wind direction at 5500 ft is 2.5° away from the
5000 ft value = 207.5°T rounded to 208°T.
Wind speed is similarly determined, a 6 kt difference in 2000 ft = 1.5kt per 500 ft.
Thus, the wind speed at 5500 ft = 13.5 = 14 kt rounded off.
So, the climb wind is 208°T/14.
The same technique is used for the ½-way down descent wind at 4500 ft near Omaka, and for the cruise wind velocities.
Headings And Groundspeeds
These are calculated using the navigation computer as shown earlier.
Instructor to demonstrate if needed.
Variation
Is taken off the VPC chart. You need to remember,
variation east - magnetic least and
variation west - magnetic best.
Headings Magnetic/Compass
Your magnetic heading is the variation applied to your HDG°T.
The compass heading is the compass deviation applied to your HDG°M.
ETAs
Using the given ETD of 2215 UTC, we can work out our ETAs for each leg, by simply adding the time onto the ETD.
Fuel Consumption
Fuel And Oil Requirements
Sufficient fuel is to be carried for the aircraft to fly from Hokitika to Omaka plus a reserve of 30 minutes.
Fuel for taxi, takeoff and climb to 1500ft- 6 litres
Climb consumption rate- 34 litres/hr
Cruise consumption rate- 28 litres/hr
Descent consumption rate- 18 litres/hr
Holding consumption rate- 24 litres/hr
Fuel required for circuit and landing- 3 litres/hr
Specific gravity of fuel- 0.72
When completing the fuel section of a flight plan you will be given the information that was on the previous page.
The fuel consumption rates and the times per sector allow us to calculate the zone fuels.
For example, from HK to TOC = 9mins at 34l/hr = 5 litres. The remaining legs are calculated using the same method.

Globe
Handout
The Minimum Fuel Required For A VFR Cross Country Flight
The minimum amount of fuel required is worked out while you do pre-flight planning.
This amount should also include the legal minimum fuel reserve for a VFR flight which is 30mins.
Do be aware, there is a minimum amount of fuel to be carried. At this stage of your flying, it is a good idea to carry as much fuel as practicable.

Globe
Handout
Maximum Range
Means flying the greatest distance on the fuel carried. Clearly then, the more fuel we carry, the greater our range.
Factors Affecting Range
Weight
Wind
Air temp
Altitude
Aircraft Config (including CSU)
Specific Range
Means the distance travelled per unit of fuel burn.
Best Specific Air Range
Found at the best TAS/Fuel Flow (FF) Ratio.
Best Specific Ground Range
Found at the best GS/FF Ratio.
Maximum Endurance
Means being able to stay airborne for the longest time possible.
Ideal for holding at an aerodrome waiting for weather to improve, as distance covered has nothing to do with endurance.
Practice Questions
Minimum Flight Time
In order to get to the destination as fast as possible.
In nil wind, highest TAS. When wind components apply, highest GS.
This cannot be achieved at the most efficient airspeed and power setting, and there must be a relatively high fuel flow.
Practice Questions

lessons.title: Radio Aids in Support of VFR Operations

content.content:
Globe
Handout
Automatic Direction Finder
The ADF is a radio receiver which, when tuned to receive the signal from a ground based non directional beacon(NDB) can indicate the direction of the NDB form the aircraft by means of a needle.
Relative Bearing
A relative bearing is the position of an object relative to the aircraft’s nose.
Calculating Magnetic Bearings To and From an NDB
Remember, a magnetic bearing is a true bearing allowing for variation.
If the NDB has a true bearing of 270°T from the aircraft and the variation is 22°E, the magnetic bearing will be 248°M.
If the aircraft has a relative bearing from the NDB of 030°T and the variation is 10°W, the magnetic bearing of the aircraft from the NDB will be 040°W.
Importance of Variation when using a VNC to Maintain Track with Reference to an ADF
Because the VNC charts are aligned to True North and the ADF is referenced to Magnetic North, if you don’t apply the variation, you will not be able to maintain the correct track.
VOR
VOR
Like the NDB, a VOR station has identifying code of two letters broadcast in morse.
It is also published on the 1:125,000 VNC charts and in the chart section of the AIP.
When using the VOR it is essential that correct station ‘ident’ is confirmed before the signals from the beacon are used.
VOR Radial
Every 360 magnetic bearing from a VOR ground station has specific phase difference which determines the radial from the VOR.
For example, when at Magnetic North from the station, you are on Radial 360, when at Magnetic South from the station, you are on Radial 180.
Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)
Primary Function of the DME
DME is a radio navigation aid designed to provide continuous indications of the aircrafts distance from the selected DME ground station.
Global Positioning System
GPS Segments
Three basic segments:
Space Segment: 24 Satellites orbiting.
Control Segment: Monitoring/Ground Antennas.
User Segment: All the receivers.
Fixing Position
4 satellites to give an accurate position
Draw picture
GPS Displays and Outputs
Draw picture
RAIM
Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring
5 Satellites required for RAIM to detect anomalous situation.
6 Satellites required to isolate the unacceptable satellite.
Coming through transit lane
PDOP
Position Dilution of Precision
The further apart the satellites are (but still in view) the lower the PDOP, and thus the greater accuracy
Draw picture
Geodetic Considerations
GPS and worldwide Data Banks use the World Geodetic System (WGS) 84.
If used in conjunction with an old chart based in the New Zealand Geodetic Datum 1949, errors of up to a couple of hundred metres may occur.
Augmentation of GPS
Ground based reference stations broadcast the difference between the position indicated by the satellites, and the known fixed ground position.
Differential GPS (DGPS) and Wide Area Augmentation System (WAAS) can reduce errors down to 3-5 metres by using ground-based reference stations.
GPS Errors and Limitations
Multi-Path Error - due to satellite signals bouncing off the Earth.
Ionospheric Propagation Effect - charged particles in ionosphere interfering with propagation speed.
Tropospheric Propagation Effect - water vapour in troposphere slowing down signals. Compensated in receiver.
Receiver Error - difficulty in matching pseudo-random code.
Interference - due to the fact satellite signals are rather weak. Insufficient shielding from VHF Radios, Radar etc.
Battery Life - generally only on portable handheld units.
Human Factors Considerations
Mode Error.
Data Entry Error.
Control Knob and Switch Non-standardisation.
Data Display.
Position in Cockpit.
Compulsive Fiddling Accuracy.
GPS as a Back-Up Navigation Tool
It is important that if you use GPS, you also have a thorough grasp of navigation skills.
It is too easy to become reliant on GPS.
GPS can fail and if the pilot has no navigational skills, they will be in serious trouble.
Radar
Radar
Two types of Radar.
New Zealand is almost covered by its two types of radar,
Primary and Secondary radar.
Principle of Information of Each Type
Primary
Primary radar works on the ‘echo’ principle, that is, signals sent out from the ground-based radar aerial strike an aircraft and scatter in all direction.
Some of these signals return to the radar aerial.
The time taken for the signals to return is a function of distance.
Principle of Information of Each Type
Primary
Secondary
Works on a slightly different principle.
The signal from the ground-based radar aerial is received by the aircraft's transponder, which sends a response signal back to the radar installation.
The time taken for the radar signal to leave the aerial and the return message from the transponder is a function of time.
Mode A and C
The transponder on light aircraft has two modes, Mode A and Mode C.
Mode A – is a 4-digit code number which is set by the pilot.
Mode C – is an additional signal which indicates the aircraft’s altitude.
Four Radar Services that may be Available to VFR Flights
Navigation Assistance
When requested, radar can advise tracks and distances to aerodromes or reporting points. Can also advise when significant distances off track and monitor aircraft’s progress over water.
Traffic Information
Information may be passed to pilots of VFR aircraft about other aircraft in the vicinity.
Weather Information
Controllers will, when possible, provide whatever information they have regarding areas of significant bad weather.
Radar Vectoring
Over the years, pilots have requested radar vectoring to get themselves out of bad situations.
If you ever find yourself in a situation and you think radar vectoring will help don’t be afraid to ask for it.
The worst thing you can do is to recognise that a dangerous situation is developing and fail to call for help.
Exam Techniques
